client: I've been really struggling since my partner passed away three months ago. Things I used to love, like going for walks or cooking a nice meal, just feel completely pointless now. I'm not sure talking about it is going to change anything, but I figured I'd give this a try.
therapist: I'm so sorry for the loss of your partner — what you're carrying right now is profound, and it makes complete sense that the things you once loved feel hollow without them. I also notice a kind of quiet exhaustion in how you're speaking, as though even the act of hoping this might help takes effort you're not sure you have right now. That skepticism is completely valid, and I just want you to know there's no pressure here — we can simply start by being present with what you're experiencing, at whatever pace feels right for you.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: Yeah, you got that right — even just showing up here today felt like a huge effort. I kept telling myself on the way over that this probably won't help, that nothing really can at this point. But I guess some small part of me is still here, so maybe that counts for something.
therapist: That small part of you that showed up today — I think that deserves more credit than you're giving it, because grief this heavy can make even the smallest act of reaching out feel like climbing a mountain. I'm curious about something you said, though — you mentioned "nothing really can help at this point," and I wonder what it would mean to you if something *did* help, even just a little?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: That's a hard question to sit with, honestly. I think part of me is afraid that if something helps, it means I'm starting to move on from them, and that feels like a kind of betrayal. Like if I stop hurting this much, maybe it means they didn't matter as much as they did.
therapist: What you just named is so important — this idea that healing feels like a betrayal is one of the most painful and common traps grief can set for us, and it makes so much sense that your love for them would show up that way. But I want to gently offer another possibility: what if carrying their memory forward *with* you, even into moments of less pain, could actually be a way of honoring how much they mattered? I'm wondering, what do you think they would have wanted for you?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: I know in my head that they would have wanted me to be okay, they were always so caring like that. But knowing that and actually feeling like it's true are two completely different things — it just sounds like something people say to make grief feel more manageable. I guess I'm not ready to use that as a reason to feel better yet, if that makes sense.
therapist: That makes complete sense, and I really respect your honesty in saying you're not ready for that yet — there's no timeline here, and forcing a comfort that doesn't feel real would only ring hollow. What I'm noticing is that even as you're putting that idea aside, there's something quite tender in the way you speak about them — "they were always so caring like that" — like their presence is still very much alive in how you see the world. Can you tell me a little more about that caring side of them?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: They had this way of just knowing when something was wrong with me, even before I said a word — they'd make tea and sit with me without making a big deal out of it. It was never dramatic, just quiet and steady, and I think that's what I miss most, that feeling of being known by someone. Talking about it now actually hurts more than I expected, like saying it out loud makes the absence more real somehow.
therapist: What you just described — that quiet, steady presence, the tea, being known without having to explain yourself — that's a profound kind of love, and it's no wonder its absence feels like something essential is missing from the world. There's something very still and tender in the way you're sharing this, like you're holding it very carefully, and I want you to know that the pain of saying it out loud doesn't mean you're doing something wrong — it means it mattered deeply. Would it feel okay to just sit with that for a moment, that this love was real and it was yours?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: I'm sitting with it, and it's... yeah, it was real. Nobody can take that away, even if it sometimes feels like losing them is slowly erasing it somehow. I didn't expect to feel both sad and something almost like grateful in the same moment — that's a strange combination I wasn't prepared for.
therapist: What you just touched on — that grief and gratitude can exist in the same breath — is actually one of the most human and healing discoveries a person can make, even when it catches us off guard. I notice something shifted just now as you said it, like the words came quickly, almost with a kind of energy underneath them. I'm curious — what does it feel like in your body right now, sitting with both of those things at once?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, very rapid speech

client: Honestly, there's this kind of tightness in my chest that's been there for months, but right now it feels slightly different — less like a wall and more like something that's just very full. It's hard to describe without sounding strange, but it's like my chest is holding both the grief and something warmer at the same time. I'm not sure I trust it yet, like maybe it'll disappear the moment I walk out of here and I'll be back to just the emptiness.
therapist: The way you described that — "less like a wall and more like something very full" — is not strange at all, it's actually quite beautiful and precise. I want to gently push back on the fear that it will disappear, because what you're noticing right now isn't something I gave you or that this room created — it came from *you*, from your willingness to speak honestly about someone you loved. What if that capacity to hold both things at once has been inside you all along, even on the hardest days?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: I want to believe that, but on most days it really doesn't feel like that capacity is there at all — it feels more like I'm just surviving hour to hour. I think what scares me is that today felt slightly different because I was talking about them, but when I go home to that quiet apartment tonight, there's no one to make tea with anymore. I don't know how to access whatever this is without them being the one who helped me find it in the first place.
therapist: The image of going home to that quiet apartment tonight is so concrete and real, and I hear how much that silence carries the weight of their absence — the tea, the steadiness, all of it. What strikes me is that you found something here today not because I was making tea, but because *you* were willing to speak their name out loud and let them be real in the room — and I wonder if that's something you might be able to offer yourself, even in small ways, on the hard nights. What do you think that could look like, even imperfectly?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: I guess maybe I could try talking about them out loud sometimes, even just to myself in the apartment — though honestly that sounds a little lonely and strange, like it might make the silence feel even louder. I'm not sure I'm the kind of person who can do that without it just turning into me falling apart completely. But I suppose falling apart isn't the worst thing, maybe.
therapist: "Falling apart isn't the worst thing, maybe" — I want to stay with that for a moment, because that's actually a quiet but significant shift from where you started today, when even being here felt like too much to hope for. There's something very gentle in the way you're holding that idea, like you're trying it on carefully rather than pushing it away entirely. And I'd gently offer that falling apart in the presence of someone you loved, even in memory, might be less like losing yourself and more like letting them witness you — the way they always did.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: That idea of letting them witness me — that actually got to me in a way I wasn't expecting, because that's exactly what they did when they were alive, they never needed me to hold it together. I think I've been trying so hard to keep myself from completely breaking down because it feels like there's no one there to catch me anymore. But maybe that's not entirely true if I carry them with me the way you're describing, even if I'm still not totally sure how that works in practice.
therapist: What you just said feels like something real and important landing inside you, and I notice there's a softness and quietness in how you're holding it — like it's tender and fragile, something you don't want to disturb too quickly. You don't have to have it all figured out today, because the understanding that they didn't need you to hold it together *is* itself a kind of catching — you just remembered something true about how they loved you. Can we let that be enough for today?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech
